doc.title: Al Gallodoro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Oneonta, New York, December 28, 2005

title: Isham Jones band, union rules and radio audition
summary: Hired by Isham Jones through Arnold Frank, let go at the Commodore for lack of a union card, then auditions for radio.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: great singer. He is at the Ritz Carlton. Don’t ask me how I got to Atlantic City from Ocean City, I must have taken a bus. I think what did we do, only 20 years old, we had no fear. And he was gone. George Olsen had gone. But at the Ambassador Hotel I see Isham Jones, oh my God, Isham Jones was a big name at that time. “It Had to be You,” “I’ll See You in my Dreams.” And the story is the same. I went to the dining room and to the maitre d’ I says, “Is it possible to see Mr. Jones?” He says, “Oh no, no, no, you can’t see him but I’ll send his manager.” Arnold Frank. Arnold Frank was his name. And he says, “All right kid.” Oh I bragged about how good I was, I had to, I had to get in. He says, “Come tomorrow afternoon” — this is good— and Jones is having a rehearsal. I had my baritone sax and my alto and clarinet. Don’t ask me how I handled the baritone sax and the clarinet and sax coming all the way from New Orleans, stopping at Knoxville, oh I stopped in Washington. That’s the first time I had ever eaten scallops. In those days Horn and Hardart had them in a pan. They were the most delicious things I had ever eaten you know. Well anyway —
Was that what they called a cafeteria style?

Yeah. It was a cafeteria. So anyway I came the next day and I played for Jones and he hired me. But the guys didn’t like me. You know why they didn’t like me? They wanted away from Jones, Jones hires me, he didn’t need me, but he only used me to solo here and there. You know who was the arranger? He became big later. Gordon Jenkins. Gordon Jenkins was the arranger. So I stayed with him until let’s say around July 7th or 8th, until after Labor Day. We toured all of New England with Jones. It was cold. There were no heaters in cars then. Finally we ended up in Manhattan. The Commodore Hotel. And that’s where Jones — I said “Gitch.” My nickname to him was “Gitch.” Why he called me “Gitch” I don’t know.

Yeah “Gitch.” I don’t know where he got that from. That was always “Gitch.” He says, “Kid I have to let you go.” I says, “Why? Am I not good enough?” He says, “No, you don’t belong to the union and you can’t work a steady job until you are here for six months.” They went into the Commodore Hotel and that’s when they had to let me go. And then I moved around, lounged around 48th Street. Musicians were up and down the street and the cops would say, “Come on guys, break it up, break it up.” And one thing led to another and you’d meet a piano player and you’d sit in or something and then he recommended me to Alfredo Antonini and Vincent Zorrie. They were the conductor and piano player at WRNS radio station. And I auditioned there and I got the job.
